Yes, a 20,000 mAh power bank is allowed on US flights, but only in your carry-on, never in checked bags.

**The math**
- The FAA limit for spare lithium-ion batteries and power banks is 100 Wh per battery. To convert, divide mAh by 1000 and multiply by the voltage ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries)).
- Most power banks use 3.7 V cells, so 20,000 mAh works out to about 74 Wh. That's under the limit.
- The Wh rating is often printed on the bank itself. If it is, go by that number.

**Rules to follow** ([FAA PackSafe: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))
- **Carry-on only:** spare lithium batteries and power banks are prohibited in checked baggage.
- **Gate checks:** if your carry-on gets checked at the gate, take the power bank out and keep it with you in the cabin.
- **Protect the terminals:** keep it in its retail packaging, a pouch, or a case, or tape over exposed terminals. This prevents short circuits.
- **Damaged or recalled banks:** don't bring them.
- **Overheating in flight:** if it gets hot, swells, or smokes, tell the crew right away.

**Check your airline.** The FAA notes that many airlines set stricter limits, including caps on how many power banks you can carry, regardless of capacity ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries)). IATA also says airline policies can differ, so confirm before you fly ([IATA](https://www.iata.org/en/youandiata/travelers/batteries/)). International flights may have additional rules.
